summary: This unit teaches you how to give first aid in a salon or spa until an ambulance or a doctor takes over. You will learn to assess a casualty with DRSABC, call for help, give CPR and use an AED, put a casualty in the recovery position, and help a choking adult. You will also learn to control bleeding and treat shock, burns, chemical splashes and electric shock, and to recognise and respond to fainting, heart attack, stroke, asthma, severe allergic reaction, low blood sugar and seizures, as well as bone and joint injuries.

blocks.p: Beauty therapists work with hot wax, sharp tools, chemicals, electrical equipment and clients lying down or sitting still for a long time. Accidents and sudden illness happen: a burn from wax, a cut from a blade, a faint, an allergic reaction or a collapse. In the first few minutes, what the people nearby do can decide whether a casualty lives, and how well she recovers.

This unit is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees. It builds your confidence to act calmly and correctly. **First aid** is the first help given to an injured or ill person before professional help arrives. Its aims are to **save life, stop the condition getting worse, and help recovery**. You learn the skills on the Centre's certified first-aid course, and you must keep your certificate up to date. This kit helps you study the knowledge; it does not replace the practical training with a manikin.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's training room: CPR with an AED trainer on a manikin and the recovery position, then scenarios for bleeding, a burn, choking, a sling and an incident report. Rescue breaths, compressions and abdominal thrusts are practised on manikins or training vests only, never on a person.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Methods change a little as first-aid guidelines are updated. Always follow the method on the Centre's certified first-aid course and the instructor. This kit gives the usual current methods for adults.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: First aid basics: the first aider, the kit and calling for help

blocks.h: The first aider's role and limits

ul: Give only the first aid that you have been trained to give. Do not try treatments you have only seen on television or social media.

You are not a doctor. Do not diagnose, and do not give medicines. The exceptions are a casualty's own prescribed medicines, such as an asthma inhaler or an adrenaline auto-injector, which you may help her to use.
Stay calm, speak clearly and reassure the casualty. A calm first aider helps everyone around her to stay calm.
Keep the casualty's dignity and privacy. Move bystanders away, and do not take photos.
Your own safety comes first. If you are injured, you cannot help anyone.

blocks.p: Before you help a conscious adult, say who you are and that you are trained, and ask if you may help. Explain what you plan to do. If she says no, respect it unless her life is in danger and she cannot decide for herself. If she is unconscious, you may help, as she would want you to. For a child, ask a parent or guardian if one is there, and help at once if there is none and the child is in danger. Ask your instructor about the law that protects a person who gives first aid in good faith.

ul: Wear **disposable gloves** when you deal with blood or body fluids. They protect both of you from infection. Use a face shield or pocket mask when you give rescue breaths.
Cover your own cuts with waterproof dressings.
Wash your hands with soap and water after you finish, even if you wore gloves.
Put soiled dressings and gloves into a clinical waste bag as the Centre's policy says.

blocks.p: Every salon and spa should have a first-aid kit that is clearly marked, easy to reach, and checked regularly. A person (the first aider) should be responsible for it.

head: Item
Use
rows: Sterile dressings and pads, in several sizes
To press on wounds and cover them
Roller bandages and triangular bandages
To hold dressings and to make slings
Adhesive plasters, waterproof, in several sizes
Small cuts and grazes
Disposable gloves (latex-free if possible)
Protection from blood and body fluids
Face shield or pocket mask
Rescue breaths with no mouth-to-mouth contact
Cling film or a sterile burn dressing
Covering a cooled burn loosely
Saline or clean water in eye wash bottles
Rinsing the eyes
Scissors, tweezers, safety pins, tape
Cutting, removing splinters and fastening bandages
Foil survival blanket
Keeping a casualty warm
Clinical waste bags and a notebook with a pen
Waste and notes for the incident record

ul: Check the kit at set times, and after each use. Replace used items, and throw away anything out of date.

Do not keep **painkiller tablets** or other medicines in a workplace kit. A first aider must not give them, and a casualty may be allergic or on other medicines. Some salons keep an eye-wash station and a burns kit near wax and chemical areas.

head: Number
Service
rows: Fire and ambulance
Police

blocks.p: Put these numbers beside the salon's phone. Call 110 for any serious injury or sudden illness: not breathing or breathing badly, unresponsive, severe bleeding, chest pain, signs of a stroke, a severe allergic reaction, a serious burn, a suspected spinal injury or a seizure that does not stop.

head: What to tell the call-taker
Example
rows: Which service you need
'Ambulance, please.'
The exact address, parish and a landmark; your phone number
'Glow Spa, 12 Main Street, Mandeville, opposite the pharmacy. 876-555-0123.'
What happened
'A client collapsed and is not breathing normally.'
How many people are hurt, their age, and their condition
'One woman, about 50; not responding.'
What you are doing
'We are giving CPR and the defibrillator is on its way.'

ul: Speak clearly and calmly. Answer the operator's questions and follow her advice. Do not hang up until she tells you to. Put the phone on speaker if you are giving CPR.
Send someone to the front of the building to meet the ambulance and guide the crew in, and to unlock gates and doors.
When the ambulance crew arrive, tell them what happened, what you found, what you did and at what times, and give any medicines or products involved. Hand over any care you were giving.

Write an **incident record** straight away: the date, time and place; who was involved; what happened; the signs; the first aid given and by whom; the time the ambulance was called and arrived; and what happened next. Do not write who was to blame, and do not guess.
Report the incident to the manager. The salon may need to inform insurers or the authorities. Keep the record private.
Replace the supplies you used. Clean the area and wash your hands.
It is normal to feel shaken afterwards. Talk to your supervisor or instructor about it.

blocks.p: **DRSABC** is the primary survey: a quick check in order for the dangers to life. Do it in this order every time. The letters stand for Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing and CPR (with defibrillation).

head: Letter
What you do
Why
rows: **D** Danger

Look for danger to you, to bystanders and to the casualty: spilled water, a faulty appliance, chemicals, fire, traffic. Make the area safe or move the danger. If you cannot, stay away and call for help.
A hurt first aider helps nobody.
**R** Response
Kneel beside her. Tap her shoulders firmly and shout, 'Can you hear me? Open your eyes.' Ask a simple question and give a simple command.
To find out whether she is conscious or unresponsive.
**S** Send for help
Shout for help. Ask a named person: 'You, please call 110 and bring the AED and the first-aid kit.' If you are alone and she is unresponsive, call yourself on speaker.
Early help saves lives; an AED needs to be on its way.
**A** Airway

Lay her on her back on a firm surface. Place one hand on her forehead and tilt her head back gently. With two fingertips under the point of her chin, lift the chin. Check inside her mouth for visible blockage.
An unresponsive casualty's tongue falls back and blocks the airway.
**B** Breathing
Look, listen and feel for **normal** breathing for **no more than 10 seconds**: watch the chest, listen at her mouth, feel for breath on your cheek.
To decide if she needs CPR.
**C** CPR
If she is not breathing normally, start chest compressions at once.
Her heart may have stopped.

blocks.note: Gasping or slow, noisy gurgling breaths in an unresponsive casualty (agonal breathing) are **not** normal breathing. They are common in the first minutes of cardiac arrest. Treat it as not breathing and start CPR.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: If she answers or moves, leave her as you found her if she is not in danger. Find out what has happened, check for injuries, and call for help if she needs it. Do a secondary survey.

The **secondary survey** is a full check, from head to toe, for other injuries, done only after the life-threatening problems are dealt with. Ask what happened and where it hurts. Look and feel gently for bleeding, swelling, deformity, burns or bruising. Check her pulse, her skin (colour, temperature, damp or dry) and any medical alert bracelet or medicines. Record what you find, and tell the ambulance crew.

If there are several casualties, **deal first with the one who is silent and not responding**, because she may not be breathing. A person who is shouting or moving is breathing and has an open airway. Treat the most life-threatening problems first, not the loudest. Call 110 and ask other people to help.
Do not move a casualty unless she is in danger, or you must reach her airway or begin CPR. Never move someone you think may have a spinal injury unless there is immediate danger.

sections.title: CPR, the AED and the recovery position

blocks.p: **Cardiac arrest** means that the heart suddenly stops pumping blood around the body. The casualty is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Without CPR, brain damage begins within minutes. It is different from a **heart attack**, in which part of the heart is short of blood but the heart is still beating and the casualty is awake.

flow: Check danger, check response, and send someone to call 110 and fetch the AED
Open the airway and check breathing for no more than 10 seconds
Kneel beside her chest; place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone)
Put the other hand on top and lock your fingers
With straight arms and your shoulders directly over your hands, press down about 5 to 6 cm
Release fully, letting the chest come back up, and keep a steady rate of about 100 to 120 a minute
After 30 compressions, give 2 rescue breaths if you are trained and willing
Carry on at 30 compressions to 2 breaths until help arrives, she moves or breathes normally, or you are too tired to continue

head: Point
Adult
rows: Hand position
Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top
Depth
About 5 to 6 cm
Rate
About 100 to 120 compressions a minute
Ratio
30 compressions to 2 breaths
Interruptions
Keep them as short as possible
Changing over
Swap with another rescuer about every 2 minutes, with the least delay

ul: **Rescue breaths**: with the airway open (head tilted, chin lifted), pinch her nose, seal your mouth over hers (or use a face shield or pocket mask) and blow steadily for about 1 second, watching the chest rise. Give 2 breaths in under 10 seconds, and return to compressions at once.
**If you cannot or will not give rescue breaths**, give **compressions only**, non-stop, at 100 to 120 a minute. Compressions alone are far better than doing nothing.

Do not stop to check for a pulse. Do not stop CPR unless she wakes up, breathes normally, a health worker takes over, the AED tells you to stop for analysis, you are exhausted, or the scene becomes unsafe.
You may hear or feel ribs crack. It can happen; keep going. Doing CPR correctly is more important than the risk of broken ribs.
Do not copy rates or depths you see in films. Learn from a manikin with an instructor.

blocks.note: Children and infants need a different rate of breaths, depth and, for infants, the hand position. Your certified course teaches these. Never improvise.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: An **AED** is a portable machine that checks the heart rhythm through two sticky pads on the chest, and gives an electric shock if the rhythm needs one. It talks you through each step. It will not shock a heart that does not need it, so it is safe for anyone to use.

flow: Send someone for the AED as soon as you know she is unresponsive and not breathing normally
Carry on CPR while the AED is brought and switched on
Bare her chest; dry it if wet; shave or cut very thick chest hair only if it stops the pad sticking
Stick the pads where the pictures show: one below the right collarbone, one on the left side below the armpit
Let the AED analyse; make sure that **everyone stands clear and nobody touches her**
If it advises a shock, check again that everyone is clear, then press the shock button
Restart compressions at once, and follow the voice prompts
Do not remove the pads or switch it off until help arrives and takes over

ul: Remove medicine patches (they can burn), and move her away from pools of water.
Do not use the AED while she is lying in water. Move her to a dry place if you can, and dry her chest.
If you see a lump under the skin on the chest (an implanted device such as a pacemaker), do not place a pad over it; place the pad a few centimetres away.
Know where your salon's AED is kept, and check that the battery and pads are within date.

blocks.p: Use it for a casualty who is **unresponsive but breathing normally**. It keeps the airway open because the tongue cannot fall back, and lets vomit or blood drain out of the mouth instead of going into the lungs.

flow: Kneel beside her as she lies on her back; remove her glasses and bulky items from her pockets
Place the arm nearest you at a right angle to her body, elbow bent, palm up
Bring her far arm across her chest and hold the back of her hand against her near cheek
With your other hand, lift her far knee, keeping the foot on the ground
Pull on the bent knee to roll her towards you onto her side
Adjust the upper leg so that the hip and knee are bent at right angles
Tilt her head back to keep the airway open, with her mouth angled downwards
Call 110 if not already done; check her breathing often; stay with her

blocks.note: If you suspect a spinal injury, do not use the recovery position unless she is not breathing normally and you cannot keep the airway open any other way, or she is vomiting. Airway comes first, always. If she stops breathing normally, turn her onto her back and start CPR.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: If she stays in the recovery position for a long time (more than about 30 minutes), turn her to the other side to ease pressure on the arm and shoulder.
Choking happens when something blocks the airway. In a salon it can happen with food, a sweet, a piece of gum or a small object. Tell the difference between a partial blockage and a complete one.

head: Mild blockage
Severe blockage
rows: She can cough, speak or breathe
She may look scared and clutch her throat
She cannot cough, speak or breathe, or makes no sound
She may go blue and become unresponsive
Encourage her to keep coughing
Stay with her and watch her
Give back blows, then abdominal thrusts

flow: Ask 'Are you choking?' If she cannot speak, act at once
Stand to her side and a little behind; support her chest with one hand and lean her well forward
Give up to **5 sharp back blows** between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand, checking after each blow whether the blockage has cleared

If not cleared, give up to **5 abdominal thrusts**: stand behind her, put your arms around her, make a fist and place it between her navel and the bottom of her breastbone, grasp it with the other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards
Check her mouth and remove anything that you can see; never sweep blindly with a finger
If still blocked, alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
Call 110 if the blockage is not cleared after the first cycle, or sooner if someone else can call
If she becomes unresponsive, lay her on her back, call 110 if not yet done, and start CPR

ul: **Do not** slap her back if she can still cough: it can push the object deeper.
**Do not** give water, food or a drink to wash it down.
**Do not** blindly put your fingers in her mouth.
Anyone who has had abdominal thrusts, even if the object came out, must see a doctor, because thrusts can injure the organs.

blocks.note: Some first-aid courses teach abdominal thrusts only, or a different order. Follow what the Centre's certified course teaches. If the casualty is pregnant, obese or a child or baby, the method changes; ask your instructor.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Do not give clients gum, sweets or food to chew while they are lying back for a treatment.
Keep small objects, pins and clips away from the mouth.
Tell clients not to eat during a treatment.

flow: Put on disposable gloves if you can get them quickly
Ask the casualty to press on the wound herself, or press with your hand
Lay her down, if she is faint or the bleeding is severe
Press firmly on the wound with a clean pad or sterile dressing
If blood soaks through, put a second pad on top and keep pressing; do not remove the first pad
When the bleeding slows, bandage the pad firmly in place, but not so tightly that the fingers or toes turn pale or cold
Call 110 for severe bleeding
Treat for shock, and watch her

ul: If it is an arm or a leg, raise it above the level of the heart (if there is no broken bone), while pressing on the wound.
**Do not** wash a severe wound, take pads off to look, or put cotton wool straight on the wound.
**If something is stuck in the wound**, such as glass or a blade: do not pull it out. Press on **either side** of it, build up padding around it, and bandage over the padding, not over the object.
Very severe bleeding that does not stop with pressure is a life-threatening emergency. Trained people may be taught to use a tourniquet. Ask your instructor; use one only if you have been trained.
Wash your hands well afterwards, and put the dressings in clinical waste.
Wash your hands and put on gloves.
Clean the wound under clean, running water; remove dirt gently.
Pat dry around the wound, and cover it with a clean waterproof plaster or dressing.
Advise her to see a doctor if the cut is deep, will not stop bleeding, has dirt in it that you cannot remove, or if she has not had a tetanus booster for ten years.
Sit her down and lean her head **forward** (not back).
Pinch the **soft part** of the nose, just below the bone, for about **10 minutes**, and ask her to breathe through her mouth.
Do not let her swallow the blood: ask her to spit it out.
After 10 minutes, release. If it is still bleeding, pinch for another 10 minutes. If it bleeds for more than 30 minutes, or after a blow to the head, get medical help.

blocks.p: **Shock** here means a life-threatening condition in which not enough blood and oxygen reach the body's organs. It can follow severe bleeding, serious burns, a heart attack or a severe allergic reaction. It is not the same as being upset or frightened.

head: Signs
What to do
rows: Pale, cold, clammy skin
Fast, weak pulse
Fast, shallow breathing
Dizziness, feeling sick, thirst
Anxiety, confusion; later she may become unresponsive
Treat the cause: stop the bleeding, cool the burn
Call 110
Lay her down; raise her legs about 30 cm if she has no leg injury
Keep her warm with a blanket
Loosen tight clothes; reassure her
Give her **nothing** to eat or drink
Check breathing often; be ready to start CPR

blocks.note: Do not let a casualty in shock walk about, sit up, or drink or eat. If she vomits or becomes unresponsive, put her in the recovery position if she is breathing normally.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Burns, chemical splashes, electric shock and eye injuries

blocks.p: In a salon, burns come from hot wax, paraffin, hot tongs and irons, hot water and steam, and chemicals. A scald is a burn from hot liquid or steam. Cooling quickly reduces the damage and the pain.

flow: Stop the treatment and remove the casualty from the heat
Cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water for about **20 minutes**
Take off rings, watches and tight things near the burn before it swells, unless they are stuck to the skin
Do not peel off wax, clothing or anything stuck to the burn
Cover loosely with cling film (laid lengthways, not wrapped round a limb) or a clean, non-fluffy dressing
Keep the casualty warm, because cooling a large area can make her cold
Call 110, or take her to a doctor, if the burn is serious

head: Get medical help urgently if...
Never...
rows: The burn is larger than the casualty's hand
It is deep, white, leathery or charred
It is on the face, hands, feet, genitals or over a joint
It goes all round a limb
It was caused by chemicals or electricity
The casualty is a child, an older person or has trouble breathing
Put ice, butter, oil, toothpaste or creams on a burn
Burst blisters
Remove stuck clothing
Use fluffy dressings or cotton wool

head: Where
What to do
rows: On the skin
Take off contaminated clothing and jewellery (wear gloves)
Rinse the area with plenty of running water for at least 20 minutes
Cover loosely; get medical help; take the product container or label with you
In the eye
Immediately rinse the eye with plenty of clean running water or an eye wash for at least 10 to 20 minutes
Hold the eyelids open; tilt the head so water flows away from the other eye
Do not rub; do not put drops in; cover with a clean pad
Get her to a doctor or hospital at once, with the product label
Swallowed
Do not make her vomit
Rinse her mouth; give sips of water only if the label or the poison centre says so
Call 110 and keep the container

blocks.note: Keep the product's safety data sheet where staff can find it. It tells you the hazards and the first aid for each chemical. In Jamaica, a poison information service may be reached through hospitals and health authorities. Ask your instructor for current numbers.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: In a salon, electric shock comes from faulty dryers, steamers, wax heaters or extension cords, often near water. Electricity can stop the heart and cause burns.

flow: Do **not touch** the casualty while she is still in contact with the electricity
Switch off at the mains or the socket, or pull out the plug
If you cannot switch off, stand on something dry and push the casualty away from the source with a dry wooden or plastic object (a broom handle, not metal)
Call 110
Check DRSABC and begin CPR if she is not breathing normally
Treat any burns, keeping them cool and covered
Everyone who has had an electric shock needs to see a doctor, even if she feels well

blocks.note: Do not touch someone who is still connected to the electricity, and do not throw water on her. Keep away from fallen power lines: stay at least a few metres away and call the electricity company and 110.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Dust or an eyelash in the eye**: do not rub. Wash your hands, sit her facing the light, and rinse the eye with clean water or saline, tilting her head with the affected eye lower.

**An object stuck in the eye, or a cut to the eye**: do not touch it or try to remove it. Place a pad around, not on, the object and bandage lightly; both eyes may need to be covered to stop movement. Call 110.
**A blow to the eye**: apply a cold compress gently, not pressing on the eye, and get medical advice.

blocks.p: Clients may become ill during a treatment. A therapist who notices early signs, stops the treatment, and acts correctly can prevent a crisis. In every case: stop the treatment, check DRSABC, call 110 when you need to, stay with the casualty and note the time.

ul: **Signs**: feeling dizzy or weak, pale and sweaty skin, blurred vision, nausea, then a short loss of consciousness.

**What to do**: lay her down flat and raise her legs, loosen tight clothing, make sure there is fresh air, and stay with her. She should recover within a minute or so. Help her up slowly and give water in sips once she is fully awake.
If she does not recover within a minute, or is not breathing normally, follow DRSABC and call 110.
Do not give coffee or a strong drink. Do not sit her upright quickly, and do not leave her alone.

**Signs**: pain or pressure in the centre of the chest (a crushing, heavy or squeezing pain) that may spread to the arm, neck or jaw; shortness of breath; sweating; nausea; a pale or grey colour; fear. Women, older people and people with diabetes may have milder or different signs, such as breathlessness, tiredness or pain in the back or stomach.

**What to do**: call 110 at once. Sit her down in the position most comfortable for her, usually half sitting with knees raised and a support behind her. Keep her calm and still. Loosen tight clothing. If she is awake and not allergic, and the ambulance operator or your training says so, she may chew one adult aspirin tablet (usually 300 mg) slowly. Do not give aspirin yourself unless your certified course allows it.
If she becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally, start CPR and use the AED.

blocks.p: A **stroke** happens when the blood supply to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel bursts. Quick treatment saves brain tissue, so act **FAST**.

head: Letter
Check
Sign of stroke
rows: **F** Face
Ask her to smile
One side of the face droops
**A** Arms
Ask her to raise both arms
One arm drifts down or she cannot lift it
**S** Speech
Ask her to say a simple sentence
Words slurred, wrong or she cannot speak
**T** Time
Note the time signs began; call 110 at once
Every minute counts

ul: Call 110, say 'stroke' and the time the signs began. Keep her comfortable, in the position she prefers, with her head and shoulders supported.
Give **nothing** to eat or drink, because swallowing may be affected. Do not give aspirin for a suspected stroke.
Watch her airway and breathing. If she becomes unresponsive and is breathing normally, place her in the recovery position.
**Signs**: wheezing, coughing, tight chest, difficulty speaking in full sentences, fast breathing. In a severe attack, blue lips, exhaustion or confusion.

**What to do**: sit her upright, leaning slightly forward; keep her calm; help her to use her own reliever inhaler, ideally with a spacer, as her asthma plan says (usually one puff at a time, taken one breath each, repeated as the plan says).
If there is no improvement in a few minutes, the attack is severe, or it is her first attack, call 110. If she becomes unresponsive, follow DRSABC.
Do not lay her flat, and do not take her inhaler away. Ask clients with asthma to bring their inhaler to every treatment.

blocks.p: **Anaphylaxis** is a sudden, life-threatening allergic reaction. In a salon it can follow contact with a product (such as hair dye or latex), a food or an insect sting. It can start within minutes.

head: Signs
What to do
rows: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat
Widespread itchy rash or hives
Difficulty breathing, wheezing, a hoarse voice
Pale, cold, clammy skin, dizziness, faintness
Feeling that something terrible is about to happen
Stop the treatment and remove the product from the skin if safe
Call 110 at once and say 'severe allergic reaction'
Help her to use her own **adrenaline auto-injector** if she has one: press it firmly against the outer middle thigh (through clothing if needed), hold it for the time on the device, and note the time
Lay her down with her legs raised; if she is struggling to breathe, let her sit up
If she has no pulse or breathing, begin CPR
If she has a second injector and has not improved after about 5 minutes, a second dose may be given, as the device instructions and the ambulance operator advise

blocks.note: A client who has had a reaction needs medical review even if she seems to recover, because the reaction can return. Always ask about allergies in the consultation, and do a patch test when the product requires it.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Hypoglycaemia** (low blood sugar) is the more common emergency. **Signs**: shaky, sweaty, pale, hungry, confused, behaving oddly, headache, then drowsy.

**What to do**: if she is awake and can swallow, give a quick sugar source such as sugary drink (not diet), glucose tablets or sweets. Repeat after about 10 to 15 minutes if she is not better, then give a snack. Let her rest.
If she is drowsy and cannot swallow, or becomes unresponsive, do **not** give anything by mouth. Call 110 and follow DRSABC.
Do not give her insulin. Ask if she has eaten and when she last checked her sugar.
**Signs**: sudden loss of awareness, stiffening, jerking movements, perhaps wetting herself, then a period of confusion.

**What to do**: note the time; keep calm and clear the space of anything that could hurt her; cushion her head with a folded jacket; loosen tight clothing near her neck. Do not hold her down. Do not put anything in her mouth.
When the jerking stops, check her breathing, put her in the recovery position and stay with her until she recovers. Be kind and protect her privacy.

Call 110 if it is her first seizure, if it lasts more than **5 minutes**, if one seizure follows another, if she is injured, has trouble breathing, or does not wake up properly. A person with known epilepsy may have a plan: follow it.

blocks.p: Jamaica's heat, hot treatment rooms, steamers and long hours without water can cause heat illness.

head: Condition
Signs
What to do
rows: Heat exhaustion
Heavy sweating, pale and clammy skin, headache, dizziness, nausea, fast pulse
Move her to a cool place, lay her down with legs raised, loosen clothes, give sips of cool water, apply cool wet cloths; she should improve in 20 to 30 minutes
Heatstroke
Very hot, red skin (may be dry or sweaty), confusion, fast pulse, collapse; the body cannot cool itself
A medical emergency: call 110, move her to a cool place, remove extra clothing, cool her quickly with cool wet cloths, a fan or cool water; do not give drinks if she is confused

head: Injury
Signs
What to do
rows: Fracture (broken bone)
Pain, swelling, bruising, a deformed limb, difficulty moving it, a grating feeling; the bone may poke through the skin
Keep the limb still, support it in the position found with padding or your hands
Cover any wound with a clean dressing and pad round a bone that is sticking out
Support an arm in a sling; keep a leg still by supporting it
Check circulation: skin colour and warmth below the injury
Do not move her unless she is in danger; call 110 for serious injuries; give nothing to eat or drink in case she needs an operation
Sprain or strain
Pain, swelling and bruising round a joint or muscle; difficulty using it
Rest; apply a cold compress (wrapped ice pack) for about 10 to 20 minutes
Light compression with a bandage; raise the limb
See a doctor if she cannot use the joint, as it may be broken
Dislocation
A joint out of place; deformity, severe pain
Do not try to put it back
Support it and get medical help

blocks.p: Do not pull a broken limb straight, ask the casualty to move it to see if it hurts, or rub it.

flow: Support the injured arm across her chest with the hand slightly higher than the elbow
Slide an open triangular bandage between her chest and her arm, with the point towards the elbow
Bring the lower end up over the arm and tie the two ends in a reef knot at the hollow above the collarbone, on the uninjured side
Tuck the point at the elbow in or pin it, so the arm is held snugly
Check that the fingertips are warm and pink; check the circulation every 10 minutes
Make sure the knot does not press on the neck bone

blocks.p: Suspect a spinal injury after a fall from a height, a hard blow to the head, or a fall in which the casualty complains of neck or back pain, numbness or tingling, or cannot move her limbs.

ul: **Keep her still.** Tell her not to move, and hold her head steady with your hands on both sides, in the position found, until the ambulance crew take over.
Call 110. Do not sit her up, roll her over or try to make her walk.
If she is unresponsive and not breathing normally, open the airway with the head tilt and chin lift gently and start CPR. Breathing comes first.
Watch for drowsiness, vomiting, a bad headache, clear fluid from the nose or ears, confusion or unequal pupils after a head injury. These need urgent medical help.
For a minor bump to the head, apply a cold compress and advise the client to see a doctor if she develops a headache, vomiting or drowsiness.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Poisoning (swallowed product)
Do not make her vomit; rinse her mouth; call 110 or the poison information service; keep the container
Splinter or small object in the skin
Wash the area; remove with clean tweezers if it is shallow and easy; cover; do not dig. See a doctor if it is deep
Bites and stings
Wash and apply a cold compress; watch for signs of severe allergy; see a doctor for bites from dogs or other animals
Fainting from heat or a hot treatment
Lay her flat with legs raised, in a cool place

ul: I can state the aims of first aid and the limits of what I am trained to do.
I can say how to get a casualty's consent and how to protect myself and her from infection.
I can list what belongs in a workplace first-aid kit, and what does not.
I can give the Jamaican emergency numbers and say what to tell the call-taker.
I can carry out DRSABC in order and say why each step matters.
I can open the airway and check breathing for no more than 10 seconds, and say why gasping is not normal breathing.
I can give adult CPR with the correct hand position, depth, rate and ratio.
I can use an AED safely and make everyone stand clear.
I can place an unresponsive, normally breathing casualty in the recovery position and say why.
I can tell mild from severe choking and give back blows and abdominal thrusts.
I can control severe bleeding, including a wound with something stuck in it.
I can recognise shock and treat it.
I can treat a burn with 20 minutes of cool running water, and say what not to put on it.
I can deal with a chemical splash, an electric shock and an eye injury safely.
I can recognise and help a casualty who is fainting, having a heart attack or a stroke (FAST), or an asthma attack.
I can recognise anaphylaxis and help a client use her adrenaline auto-injector.
I can treat low blood sugar in a conscious casualty, and care for someone having a seizure.
I can recognise heat exhaustion and heatstroke and say how they differ.
I can support a broken limb, make a sling, and care for a casualty with a suspected spinal injury.
I can hand over to the ambulance crew and write an accurate incident record.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. Example: 'I cool the burn under running water for 20 minutes because this stops the heat damaging deeper tissue and eases the pain.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The first help given to an injured or ill person before professional help arrives.
Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR: the primary survey.
The quick first check for life-threatening problems.
The head-to-toe check for other injuries, done after the life-saving checks.
Not responding to voice or touch.
The route air takes through the mouth, nose and throat to the lungs.
The method of opening the airway of an unresponsive casualty lying on her back.
When the heart suddenly stops pumping blood around the body.
When part of the heart is short of blood; the heart is still beating.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions, with or without rescue breaths.
Pressing down on the centre of the chest to keep blood moving.
Automated external defibrillator: a machine that checks the heart rhythm and gives a shock if needed.
A life-size practice doll used to learn CPR.
A device placed over the casualty's face so that rescue breaths can be given without mouth-to-mouth contact.
The position on her side that keeps the airway of an unresponsive, breathing casualty open.
Sharp blows between the shoulder blades to dislodge a blockage.
Inward and upward thrusts above the navel to clear a blockage.
Pressing firmly on a wound with a clean pad to stop bleeding.
A life-threatening condition in which not enough blood and oxygen reach the organs.
A burn caused by hot liquid or steam.
A device that injects a dose of adrenaline into the thigh in anaphylaxis.
A blockage or bleed in the brain; FAST: Face, Arms, Speech, Time.
A sudden episode of abnormal brain activity, causing loss of awareness and often jerking.
A dangerous condition in which the body overheats and cannot cool itself.
A large triangle of cloth used for slings and to hold dressings.
A written account of an accident or emergency and the first aid given.

c1.title: A client collapses in Mandeville
c1.text: At a spa in Mandeville, therapist Natalie is giving a back massage to Mr Everton Lewis, 58. He suddenly goes limp and does not respond when she shakes his shoulders and calls his name. His chest is not moving normally; he makes an occasional slow, noisy gasp. Another therapist, Andre, is at reception. The spa has a defibrillator (AED) in a cabinet by the door. The spa is on the first floor, and the front door is locked.

c2.title: A deep cut at a nail desk in St Ann's Bay
c2.text: A trainee, Shadae, drops a pair of scissors, and they cut across the palm of Mrs Olive Pryce's hand. Blood is flowing quickly. Mrs Pryce is pale and shaky. The first-aid kit is in the back room.

c3.title: A hot-wax burn in Linstead
c3.text: In a salon in Linstead, therapist Kerry-Ann spills a pot of hot wax on the forearm of her client, Miss Natasha Ellis. The wax sticks to the skin, which is red and beginning to blister. Miss Ellis is crying. The client is wearing a ring and a watch on that arm. A co-worker suggests putting ice and toothpaste on the burn.

c4.title: A choking client in Spanish Town
c4.text: During her break at a salon in Spanish Town, client Mrs Hyacinth Brown, 61, eats a piece of hard candy while waiting. She suddenly grabs her throat. She cannot speak or cough, and her lips are turning blue. Trainee Rohan, who has been trained in first aid, is next to her. Another client wants to give her a glass of water.

c5.title: A swollen face in Montego Bay
c5.text: Ten minutes after a new eyelash glue was applied, client Miss Shelly-Ann Reid, 29, says that her face feels tight and her lips feel big. Her eyelids are swollen, she has red blotches on her neck, and she is wheezing. She says she has a pen-like injector in her bag because she is allergic to peanuts. The therapist, Kimone, is alone with her.

c6.title: A faint and a fall at the Centre in Kingston
c6.text: During a practical session at the Centre's salon in Kingston, a trainee, Tishana, goes pale and sweaty, and says she feels dizzy. She has a known diabetes diagnosis and skipped breakfast. A moment later she sways and slides to the floor, but she is awake and can talk. A second trainee, Devon, slips on a wet floor near the basin and lands heavily on his wrist, which is swollen and painful.

questions.q: Mr Lewis does not respond and is not breathing normally. What should Natalie do straight away?
o: Send Andre for 110, the AED and the front door, then open the airway
Leave him and run downstairs to look for a doctor in the building
Roll him onto his front to look for injuries before calling anyone
Begin rescue breaths at once, before anyone has called for help
questions.why: After checking for danger and response, send a named person for help and the AED, then open the airway. Help and the defibrillator must be on their way as early as possible, and the front door must be open for the crew.

questions.q: Natalie hears a slow, noisy gasp every few seconds. How should she treat this?
o: As normal breathing, so she puts him in the recovery position
As a sign that he is waking, so she keeps talking to him
As a sign that he is choking, so she gives back blows
As not breathing normally, so she starts CPR
questions.why: Occasional slow, noisy gasps (agonal breathing) are common in the first minutes of cardiac arrest and are not normal breathing. Start CPR and use the AED.

questions.q: After about two minutes of compressions Natalie is tiring, and Andre offers to take over. What is the best way to change over?
o: Natalie stops for a minute to rest and then Andre starts compressions
Natalie carries on alone, because stopping risks harm to Mr Lewis
Andre takes over at the end of the next cycle, with a very short pause
Andre waits and takes over only when the ambulance crew arrive
questions.why: Rescuers should swap about every two minutes, because tiredness makes compressions shallow, and the pause should be as short as possible. Swapping at the end of a cycle keeps interruptions to a minimum.

questions.q: The AED analyses his heart and says 'No shock advised.' What should Natalie do?
o: Remove the pads and switch the AED off, since it has found nothing wrong
Restart CPR at once and follow the AED prompts
Wait and see whether he starts breathing before touching him again
Switch the AED off and give rescue breaths only for two minutes
questions.why: 'No shock advised' does not mean the casualty is well. He still needs chest compressions. Keep the pads on, follow the prompts and carry on until the crew arrive or he starts to breathe normally.

questions.q: There are no gloves in sight, and the first-aid kit is in the back room. What is the best first action for Shadae?
o: Press on the wound with a clean pad now, and send someone for the kit
Wait for someone to bring gloves before touching the wound at all
Wash the wound in the sink first to see how deep the cut really is
Wrap a towel loosely round the hand and wait for the bleeding to stop
questions.why: Bleeding must be controlled at once with direct pressure; the casualty can press on it herself while help fetches the kit. Washing a bleeding wound or a loose wrap wastes time. Wash your hands after, and put on gloves when you have them.

questions.q: Mrs Pryce is pale and says she feels dizzy. What should Shadae do?
o: Sit her upright and give her a glass of cold water to sip slowly
Help her to walk around the salon to get her colour back
Give her a sugary drink and a chair by the window to sit in
Lay her down, keep her warm and give her nothing to drink
questions.why: Pale skin and dizziness after bleeding may mean shock. Lay her down, raise her legs if possible, keep her warm and give nothing by mouth, in case she needs a procedure. Call 110 for severe bleeding.

questions.q: Once the bleeding has slowed, Shadae bandages the pad. How can she check that the bandage is not too tight?
o: Ask whether the hand feels hot, and loosen it if she says that it does
Check that the knot is on top of the pad and not on the wound edge
Check the fingertips stay warm and pink; loosen it if they go pale
Check that the bandage covers the whole hand and wrist, with no gaps
questions.why: A bandage should hold the pad firmly but not cut off the circulation. Pale, cold, blue or tingling fingertips mean it is too tight and must be loosened, and then rechecked.

questions.q: The wax has hardened on Miss Ellis's burned skin. What should Kerry-Ann do?
o: Peel it off quickly while the burn is still hot, so it cannot stick
Leave the wax on and cool the area under running water
Scrape it off with a spatula first, then cool the skin under water
Rub it off with baby oil first and then cool the skin afterwards
questions.why: Pulling off wax that is stuck to a burn can tear the skin. Cool the area under running water for about 20 minutes and let the wax come away on its own or be removed by a doctor.

questions.q: Why should Kerry-Ann take off Miss Ellis's ring and watch early, unless they are stuck?
o: The arm will swell and a tight ring can cut off the blood
They may be spoiled by the water used to cool the burn
They may pass heat from the burn on to the rest of the arm
They will stop the cooling water from reaching the burned skin
questions.why: Burned areas swell quickly. A ring or watch can become tight and cut off circulation, so remove it early, unless it is stuck to the skin, in which case leave it for medical staff.

questions.q: After 20 minutes of cooling, the burn is covered with cling film laid lengthways. What is the main reason for using cling film?
o: It keeps the burn hot so that the skin heals faster
It can be wrapped tightly to stop the burn from swelling up
It lets the client rub in cream through the film as it dries
It does not stick to the burn and keeps it clean
questions.why: Cling film is clean, does not stick, and lets the burn be seen. Lay it loosely, not wrapped round a limb, because swelling could make it tight.

questions.q: Mrs Brown cannot speak or cough, and her lips are turning blue. How should Rohan position her for the back blows?
o: Lay her flat on the floor on her back, with her head tilted back
Stand her upright with her head tilted back to open the throat
Stand at her side, support her chest and lean her well forward
Sit her in a low chair with her hands on her head to widen the chest
questions.why: Leaning her forward means the object can fall out of her mouth rather than slide further down. Support her chest with one hand and give sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the other.

questions.q: Why should Rohan not accept the other client's offer of a glass of water?
o: Water would make the candy dissolve more slowly in her throat
She cannot swallow, so water could go into her airway
The water could be too cold for a person who is in shock
Water will be needed later to treat her and should be saved
questions.why: A casualty with a severe blockage cannot swallow, and liquid can enter the airway. Act at once with back blows and thrusts.

questions.q: The candy shoots out after the abdominal thrusts, and Mrs Brown says she feels fine. What should Rohan advise?
o: That she should see a doctor, since thrusts can injure organs
That she is fine because the airway is clear, and she can go home
That she should eat something soft to settle her stomach after the shock
That she should drink plenty of water straight away to soothe her throat
questions.why: Anyone who has had abdominal thrusts should be checked by a doctor, because thrusts can cause internal injury. Record what happened.

questions.q: Which action is best for Kimone to take first?
o: Rinse off the glue and wait to see whether the swelling goes down
Give her an antihistamine tablet from her own bag and watch her
Lay her flat, cover her with a blanket and let her rest quietly
Call 110 and help her use her own adrenaline auto-injector
questions.why: Swelling of the face and eyes, a rash and wheezing show anaphylaxis, which can quickly become fatal. Call 110 at once and help her to use her injector. Giving a tablet or waiting wastes time.

questions.q: Where on the body does Kimone press the auto-injector?
o: Into the top of the upper arm, near the shoulder joint
Into the stomach, just below the ribs, pressing firmly
Into the outer middle of the thigh, through clothes
Into the side of the neck, where the pulse can be felt
questions.why: The outer middle thigh has a large muscle that absorbs the adrenaline well. Press firmly, hold for the time shown on the device, and note the time of the dose.

questions.q: After the injection, Miss Reid feels better and wants to go home. What should happen?
o: She can go home if a friend takes her and stays with her
She should still go to hospital, because the reaction can return
She can go home to rest, because the reaction is now over
She can go back to work after drinking some water and resting
questions.why: The effect of adrenaline wears off, and a second reaction can follow. Anyone treated for anaphylaxis needs to be seen at hospital.

questions.q: Tishana drinks some sugary juice, but after 15 minutes she is still shaky and confused. What next?
o: Give more sugar, and call 110 if she is not improving
Give her a large meal and leave her to sleep it off
Give her a glass of plain water and wait ten more minutes
Ask her to walk around the room to improve her circulation
questions.why: If one dose of sugar has not worked, repeat it and get medical help if she does not improve. Once she is better, give a snack. Never leave her alone.

questions.q: Tishana becomes drowsy and cannot swallow safely. What should Devon do?
o: Give small sips of juice through a straw to keep her sugar up
Put sugar under her tongue and wait for her to improve
Pour juice slowly into her mouth while she lies on her back
Call 110, give nothing by mouth, and follow DRSABC
questions.why: An unconscious or drowsy casualty can choke on food or drink. Call 110, keep her airway safe and give nothing by mouth.

questions.q: Devon's wrist is swollen and painful, and he says it hurts to move it. What should be done?
o: Pull gently on the hand to straighten the wrist again
Ask him to rotate the wrist to see how badly it is hurt
Support it as found, apply a wrapped cold pack and get help
Rub it with oil and wrap it tightly with a firm bandage
questions.why: A painful, swollen wrist may be broken. Support it, use a cold pack wrapped in cloth, and see a doctor. Moving, pulling or rubbing it can do more harm.

questions.q: A client under a steamer in a hot room becomes confused. Her skin is hot and red, and she has stopped sweating. What is the most important action?
o: Give her a hot drink and a blanket to stop her shivering
Call 110, move her somewhere cool and cool her with wet cloths
Wait 30 minutes for her to cool off before deciding on a call
Give her a cold drink and let her sleep it off in the chair
questions.why: Hot skin, confusion and no sweating suggest heatstroke, a medical emergency. Call 110 and cool her at once. Do not give drinks to someone who is confused.
